title: Tellen — van nul tot honderd
summary: Numbers 0–100, the -tien teens, and the reversed tens (vierentwintig)

blocks.title: The building blocks: 0–12
blocks.body: The first twelve are their own words — learn them cold and the rest is Lego. Watch *een* (one), which is also the word for 'a'; context tells you which.

blocks.title: The teens: just add -tien
blocks.body: From 13 up, glue the unit onto **-tien** (like English -teen). Two spelling quirks: 13 is *dertien* (not 'drietien') and 14 is *veertien* (not 'viertien'). The rest are regular.

blocks.title: The tens
blocks.body: The round tens end in **-tig**. Same two quirks return: *dertig* (30) and *veertig* (40). Note *tachtig* (80) picks up an extra t at the front.

blocks.title: The famous reversed tens
blocks.body: This is the one everybody trips on. Dutch says the **unit first**, then *en*, then the ten — all as **one word**. So 24 is *vierentwintig* (literally 'four-and-twenty'). Think of the nursery rhyme 'four and twenty blackbirds' and you've got the pattern.
blocks.callout: *tweeëntwintig* (22) and *drieëntwintig* (23) get a trema (¨) so the two e's don't blur: twee-en → *tweeën*.

blocks.explain: Unit first: *vier* (4) + *en* + *twintig* (20) = 24. The reverse, 42, would be *tweeënveertig*.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type the number as a Dutch word.
Write the number 47 as one Dutch word.
blocks.hint: Unit + en + ten, all glued together.

blocks.prompt: Write out your age and your house number in Dutch words. Then count from 20 to 30 out loud — feel the reversed pattern kick in.
